full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. XXX (G.R. No. 260860), ACCUSED-APPELLANT.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
topics: Appeal by the accused waives double jeopardy, including the implied acquittal of the greater offense (absolute waiver)
Appellate court may convict of the original, graver charge (Rule 124, Sec. 11)
Defect in the date alleged in the Information is waived if not raised before arraignment
Consummated statutory rape of a child: pain and attempted penetration (People v. Agao)

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Constitutional Rights > S. Right Against Double Jeopardy

other_subjects.subject: Criminal Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > H. Title VIII – Crimes Against Persons

doctrine:
**When the accused appeals a conviction for a lesser offense, he waives the constitutional safeguard against double jeopardy both as to that conviction and as to the implied acquittal of the original (greater) charge. The whole case is thrown open to review, and the appellate court may convict him of the original charge** (here, statutory rape instead of acts of lasciviousness). The Court reiterated the "absolute waiver" theory consistently applied in Philippine jurisprudence (Trono v. United States; Ko Bu Lin v. CA; People v. Carreon; People v. Rondero, all citing Lontoc v. People), which is reflected in Rule 124, Section 11 (the CA may "increase or reduce the penalty"). The rule that a "downgraded" conviction can no longer be reviewed applies only when the **State** appeals (Kepner; People v. Dela Torre) or, as in People v. Alarcon, in an automatic review in which the accused had no hand. The Court clarified that People v. Arcega (a State appeal) erred in relying on People v. Balunsat (an accused's appeal), and noted that the Balunsat doctrine had already been abandoned (People v. XXX262846, G.R. No. 262846, February 18, 2025, En Banc).

An Information alleging that rape was committed "on or about the year 2015" is defective: under People v. Ladrillo it covers the year and the years immediately before and after, so the accused must account for up to 36 months. The remedy is a motion for bill of particulars or a motion to quash because the Information does not conform substantially to the prescribed form (Rule 117, Sec. 3(e)). The Court clarified that **a defective information is not "cured" by evidence at trial. It is quashed, amended, or waived.** This ground is not among the non-waivable grounds in Rule 117, Section 9, so it is waived if not raised before arraignment and cannot be raised for the first time on appeal.

On consummation, the Court reiterated People v. Agao (En Banc, 2022). "Mere touching" means the penis penetrating the cleft of the labia majora, however slightly. With pre-pubescent victims, an attempt to penetrate likely indicates at least introduction into the vulval cleft. Where a child does not explicitly describe penetration, courts may find consummation from attendant circumstances, such as the victim's testimony that she felt pain in her genitals.
facts:
AAA was born on March 7, 2006. Her mother cohabited with accused-appellant XXX and had a daughter with him. When the mother left to work in Qatar, XXX cared for AAA, who called him "Papa." XXX was charged with two counts of qualified rape (as AAA's stepfather) under two Informations. Criminal Case No. 17-0678 alleged rape "on or about the 5th day of July 2017," when AAA was 11. Criminal Case No. 17-0904 alleged rape "[on] or about the year 2015," when AAA was nine. XXX pleaded not guilty. He did not move to quash either Information or ask for a bill of particulars.

AAA testified about the first rape in June 2015 and the last on July 5, 2017. On cross-examination about 2015 she answered that he was not able to insert his penis ("Hindi po"). On redirect she said he was pushing it ("Tinutulak niya po") and that she was hurt. Elsewhere she testified "pinilit niya pong ipasok" and "nasaktan po" for both incidents. AAA reported the abuse to a teacher on July 7, 2017. The medico-legal officer found redness on the peri-hymenal region, clear evidence of blunt penetrating trauma to the hymen, and shallow healed lacerations. XXX raised denial and alibi.

The RTC's Joint Judgment convicted XXX of statutory rape for the July 5, 2017 incident. The qualifying circumstance of relationship was not proved because there was no proof that XXX was married to AAA's mother. He was sentenced to reclusion perpetua and ordered to pay PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages. For the 2015 incident, the RTC convicted him only of acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the RPC in relation to Section 5(b) of RA 7610, because it found no penile penetration. It awarded PHP 50,000.00 for each kind of damages.

On XXX's appeal, the CA affirmed (June 23, 2021 Decision, CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 13804). The CA said that pain indicates penetration. However, relying on People v. Arcega, it held that XXX could no longer be convicted of rape for 2015 without violating double jeopardy, since the RTC's ruling was practically an acquittal of rape. XXX appealed to the Supreme Court. He invoked Ladrillo against the "year 2015" allegation and attacked AAA's competence and consistency.
issues: Whether the Information in Criminal Case No. 17-0904, alleging that the rape was committed "on or about the year 2015," violated accused-appellant's right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation, and whether he may raise the defect on appeal.
Whether the alleged inconsistencies in AAA's testimony impair her credibility.
Whether the 2015 incident was consummated rape rather than acts of lasciviousness.

Whether accused-appellant may be convicted of statutory rape for the 2015 incident, even though the RTC convicted him only of acts of lasciviousness, without violating his right against double jeopardy.
ruling:
**1. The Information was defective, but the defect was waived.** AAA's sworn statement gave the date as June 2015, so the Court found it "inexcusable" that the State alleged "on or about the year 2015" and not "in or about June 2015." Under Ladrillo, such an allegation covers the year and the immediately prior and subsequent years. In United States v. Dichao, an interval of 22 months was already too indefinite, so 36 months is more so. The Court distinguished Magbanua, Santos, and Gianan. It rejected the statements in Cantomayor and Gianan that such a defect may be cured by the evidence: "an information's validity cannot be determined based on the evidence presented in a case"; "[s]trictly speaking, any defect in the information is not cured by evidence presented during trial. The defective information is only either quashed, directed to be amended, or waived." By going to arraignment without moving to quash or for a bill of particulars, accused-appellant waived the objection. Lack of conformity with the prescribed form is not among the four non-waivable grounds in Rule 117, Section 9, so **it was "too late in the day" to raise it on appeal.**

**2. No.** Inconsistencies on minor details that do not touch the central fact of the crime do not impair credibility. They bolster it by discounting the possibility of rehearsed testimony. Youth and immaturity are badges of truth and sincerity. The quoted portions of AAA's testimony cannot be taken in isolation from the rest of it.

**3. Yes, the 2015 incident was consummated rape.** Applying People v. Agao, the Court explained that "mere touching" means penetration of the cleft of the labia majora, however slight. Given the underdeveloped genitalia of a pre-pubescent child, an attempt to penetrate is likely indicative of introduction into the vulval cleft. Agao also directs courts to look at attendant circumstances, such as pain in the genitals, bleeding, redness, absent hymenal tags, or other injury, and to give due regard to a child's linguistic limitations. Viewed this way, AAA's statements "pinilit niya pong ipasok," "tinutulak niya po," and "nasaktan po" proved beyond reasonable doubt that rape was consummated in 2015 as well as in 2017, contrary to the RTC's finding.

**4. Yes. Double jeopardy is no bar because the accused himself appealed.** The CA relied on Arcega, which cited Balunsat, which cited Alarcon, which cited Dela Torre. Arcega was a State appeal and correctly barred the prosecution from assailing the acquittal, but it erred in citing Balunsat, where the accused appealed. The limitation in Balunsat applies only to prosecution appeals, and that doctrine has been abandoned. Alarcon was an automatic review and Dela Torre a prosecution appeal. Neither involved an accused's own appeal. Following Trono v. United States, when the accused appeals "the government had no voice in the matter of the appeal; it simply followed" him, and he "must take the burden with the benefit." The US Supreme Court rejected this "absolute waiver" theory in Green v. United States (1957). The Philippine Court, however, has consistently applied it (Ko Bu Lin, Carreon, Rondero, Lontoc), and Rule 124, Section 11 lets the CA increase the penalty. In cases such as San Andres, Solar, Ladra, and Perez, the Court convicted the accused of the graver original charge on appeal. The purpose of double jeopardy is to prevent government oppression, "not to frustrate justice"; the Court "could not claim to be dispensers of justice if Our power of review would be limited to 'downward' corrections of error." **Because accused-appellant's own appeal threw the whole case open, there was no bar to convicting him of statutory rape instead of acts of lasciviousness, whether by the CA or by the Supreme Court.**
disposition: The appeal was DISMISSED. The CA's June 23, 2021 Decision in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 13804 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION: XXX was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of two counts of statutory rape and sentenced to reclusion perpetua for each count. He was ordered to pay AAA PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages for each count, all with legal interest of 6% per annum from finality of the Decision until fully paid.

bar_questions.q: Romeo was charged with statutory rape of his live-in partner's eight-year-old daughter. The child testified that Romeo "pinilit ipasok" his penis into her vagina and that she was hurt, but on cross-examination she answered "hindi po" when asked whether it went in. The RTC convicted Romeo only of acts of lasciviousness in relation to Section 5(b) of RA 7610, finding no penetration. Romeo alone appealed. The Court of Appeals found that rape was consummated and convicted him of statutory rape. Romeo argues that the RTC's judgment was an implied acquittal of rape and that convicting him of rape on his own appeal violates his right against double jeopardy. Is Romeo correct?

alac.answer: No. By appealing, Romeo waived his right against double jeopardy, including as to the implied acquittal of rape. The CA could validly convict him of statutory rape.
alac.legal_basis: When an accused appeals a conviction for a lesser offense, he waives the constitutional safeguard against double jeopardy both as to that conviction and as to the implied acquittal of the original charge. The whole case is thrown open to review, and the appellate court may render the judgment that law and justice dictate, including conviction for the original charge (Rule 124, Sec. 11). The bar against reviewing a downgraded conviction applies only when the State appeals. On consummation, "mere touching" means penetration of the cleft of the labia majora, however slight, and a child's testimony of pain while the offender tried to penetrate supports a finding of consummated rape (People v. Agao). (People v. XXX, G.R. No. 260860, November 11, 2025, En Banc)
alac.application: The appeal was taken by Romeo alone; the State merely followed him to the CA. Having asked the CA to review the judgment, Romeo cannot limit his waiver to the part he dislikes and use the implied acquittal as a shield. The child's testimony that Romeo forced his penis in and that she was hurt, read as a whole and with due regard to her limited vocabulary, shows at least penetration of the labial cleft. Her answer of "hindi po" on cross-examination does not negate this.
alac.conclusion: Romeo's appeal opened the whole case to review, so his conviction for statutory rape by the CA does not violate double jeopardy.

bar_questions.q: Same facts as above, except that Romeo did not appeal his conviction for acts of lasciviousness. Instead, the People, through the OSG, appealed to the Court of Appeals, arguing that the evidence proved consummated statutory rape and that Romeo should be convicted of rape and sentenced to reclusion perpetua. Should the CA give due course to the People's appeal?

alac.answer: No. The People's appeal would place Romeo in double jeopardy and must be dismissed.
alac.legal_basis: The prosecution cannot appeal a judgment in a criminal case to reverse an acquittal or to increase the penalty imposed in a conviction. A conviction for a lesser offense is an implied acquittal of the greater offense charged, and an appeal by the State to review that downgrading violates the right against double jeopardy (People v. Dela Torre; Kepner v. United States). In People v. XXX (G.R. No. 260860, November 11, 2025, En Banc), the Court explained that this bar applies only when the State appeals. It does not apply when the accused himself appeals and thereby waives the protection.
alac.application: Unlike in the previous problem, the appeal here is at the instance of the State, not Romeo. Romeo has not waived anything; he accepted the judgment. The People's appeal seeks to reverse Romeo's implied acquittal of rape and to increase his penalty, which is exactly what double jeopardy forbids. Whether or not the evidence actually showed penetration does not matter.
alac.conclusion: The CA should dismiss the People's appeal because it seeks to review an implied acquittal and increase the penalty, in violation of double jeopardy.

bar_questions.q: Pablo was charged with rape in an Information alleging that the crime was committed "on or about the year 2019." The complainant's sworn statement, attached to the complaint, stated that the rape happened in March 2019. Pablo was arraigned and pleaded not guilty without filing any motion. After conviction, he argued on appeal for the first time that the Information violated his right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation, because it forced him to account for his whereabouts over several years. (a) Was the Information defective, and what remedies were available to Pablo before arraignment? (b) Will his argument on appeal prosper?

alac.answer: (a) Yes, the Information was defective for indefiniteness as to the date. Pablo could have moved for a bill of particulars or moved to quash because the Information did not conform substantially to the prescribed form. (b) No. He waived the defect by not raising it before arraignment.
alac.legal_basis: An allegation that a crime was committed "on or about" a given year covers the year and the immediately prior and subsequent years, which is too indefinite to let the accused prepare his defense (People v. Ladrillo). The remedy is a motion for bill of particulars or a motion to quash under Rule 117, Section 3(e). Under Rule 117, Section 9, failure to assert a ground before pleading is a waiver, except for the grounds in paragraphs (a), (b), (g), and (i) of Section 3. A defective information is not cured by evidence at trial; it is quashed, amended, or waived. (People v. XXX, G.R. No. 260860, November 11, 2025, En Banc)
alac.application: Since the sworn statement said March 2019, the prosecution should have alleged "in or about March 2019." Alleging only the year exposed Pablo to a period of up to three years, so the Information was open to a motion for bill of particulars or a motion to quash under Rule 117, Section 3(e). But Pablo entered his plea without raising either. Non-conformity with the prescribed form is not one of the non-waivable grounds, so by pleading he in effect accepted that the Information sufficiently informed him of the charge.
alac.conclusion: The Information was defective, but Pablo waived the defect by pleading without objection, so he can no longer raise it on appeal.

notes: The abandonment of People v. Balunsat was not done in this case. The main opinion cites People v. XXX262846 (G.R. No. 262846, February 18, 2025, Per J. Kho, Jr., En Banc) for it. This case applied the abandonment and pointed out the error in People v. Arcega. Leonen, SAJ. filed a separate opinion and Kho, Jr., J. a concurring opinion; neither was used for the doctrine. The two Informations charged qualified rape by a stepfather, but the RTC found relationship unproved because there was no proof of marriage to AAA's mother; the qualifier was not revived on appeal.
